text: Every pool in the last four lessons spread an LP's capital across the entire price curve, from zero to infinity — even though an asset pair usually trades in a narrow band. Concentrated liquidity lets an LP deposit only where the price actually is.

Full-range liquidity spreads capital across the whole curve, so most of it sits at prices that will realistically never be reached. A concentrated position puts the same dollar amount only inside a chosen range, so all of it sits where price actually trades.

A full-range LP might have only one or two percent of their capital actively earning fees near the current price. A concentrated LP depositing the same total amount into a tight range can provide the same fee-earning depth using roughly ten to twenty times less capital.

If price moves outside your chosen range, your position converts entirely into whichever asset is now cheaper, and you stop earning fees until price re-enters. Concentrated liquidity management is an active, ongoing decision, not deposit-and-forget.
More fee income when price behaves, zero fee income when it doesn't. Next up: Chapter 3 moves to lending and borrowing, starting with how overcollateralization actually works.
